art-1792565875311-7tnfp6.title_original: Cooperative Bank of Oromia Reports ETB 11.47 Billion Pre-Tax Profit
art-1792565875311-7tnfp6.raw_text:
The Cooperative Bank of Oromia (Coopbank) posted a profit before tax of ETB 11.47 billion for the 2025/26 fiscal year. The bank reported the results at its 22nd Ordinary General Assembly of Shareholders.

At the meeting, shareholders reviewed the bank’s annual performance and strategic priorities. Total deposits reached ETB 193.26 billion, and foreign exchange earnings for the year came to USD 570.8 million.

Digital banking was among the bank’s strongest areas. Its mobile money platform, Coopay E-birr, has 22.3 million users and has processed ETB 2.74 trillion in digital transactions. Through its Michu digital lending product, the bank has disbursed more than ETB 60 billion across about 3.169 million loan accounts.

Coopbank also continued to support Ethiopia’s agricultural sector. It disbursed more than ETB 6 billion in agricultural financing to over 67,000 farmers.

The Assembly reaffirmed Coopbank’s commitment to financial innovation, inclusive growth, and sustainable value for its shareholders, customers, and communities.

The post Cooperative Bank of Oromia Reports ETB 11.47 Billion Pre-Tax Profit appeared first on StockMarket.et.

art-1792565875311-oqgruv.title_original: Ethio Telecom Board Appoints Tariku Demissie as Acting Chief Executive Officer
art-1792565875311-oqgruv.raw_text:
The Board of Directors of Ethio Telecom has appointed Mr. Tariku Demissie as Acting Chief Executive Officer of the company, effective October 16, 2026.

The appointment was communicated in a letter issued by Ms. Frehiwot Tamiru, Chairperson of the Board of Directors. Ms. Frehiwot previously served as Chief Executive Officer of Ethio Telecom. On October 8, 2026, Prime Minister Dr. Abiy Ahmed appointed her Minister of Innovation and Technology.

In the letter, the Chairperson stated that the company has developed and begun implementing a three-year strategic plan entitled Next Horizon: Digital and Beyond 2028. She noted that the first year of the plan was concluded with significant success.

Ms. Frehiwot described the present period as a critical juncture for the company. Ethio Telecom is implementing the second year of its strategy while undergoing a change in its top leadership. She stated that three matters require focused attention: an orderly leadership transition, the uninterrupted continuity of the company’s operations and services, and the further strengthening of capacities already built.

Accordingly, the Board has entrusted Mr. Tariku with responsibility for ensuring the effective implementation of the strategic plan, in coordination with the company’s management, staff and relevant stakeholders. His mandate also covers:

  • directing day-to-day operations through appropriate leadership oversight and control;
  • improving service quality and operational efficiency; and
  • strengthening the company’s sustainable growth and competitiveness.

The letter did not specify the duration of the acting appointment or a timeline for the appointment of a permanent Chief Executive Officer.

Source: Tikvah Ethiopia

The post Ethio Telecom Board Appoints Tariku Demissie as Acting Chief Executive Officer appeared first on StockMarket.et.

art-1792565875311-hu17gi.title_original: Dangote Brings Africa’s Biggest IPO to Addis, Promises ‘No Limit’ on his Investment to Ethiopia
art-1792565875311-hu17gi.raw_text:
Aliko Dangote, Africa’s richest man, told Ethiopian investors on Thursday that his group’s commitment to Ethiopia “has no limit,” as shares in his giant Nigerian oil refinery were formally opened to qualified Ethiopian buyers for the first time.

Speaking at the Dangote IPO Ethiopia Investor Roadshow, hosted by the Ethiopian Securities Exchange (ESX) at the Ethiopian Skylight Hotel, Dangote framed the moment as personal as much as commercial. “I am actually a citizen of Ethiopia,” he told a hall of bankers, investors, regulators and government officials.

Dangote Petroleum Refinery and Petrochemicals is selling 4.1 billion shares in what is billed as Africa’s largest-ever initial public offering. Ethiopian qualified investors can now subscribe at ETB 74.90 per share until 23 October.

“Whatever we make here, we will bring more and more here”

Dangote used the stage to lay out his group’s Vision 2030, under which it plans to invest $50 billion and grow revenue to $100 billion by 2030. Ten percent of that investment across Africa, he said, is earmarked for Ethiopia, and the country should expect even more.

“The investment in Ethiopia has no limit,” he said. “Whatever we make here, we will bring more and more here.”

In one of the evening’s biggest announcements for the local market, Dangote said 10% of the group’s Ethiopian fertilizer business will be listed on the ESX. The group is building a $2.5 billion urea complex in Gode, Somali Region, in partnership with Ethiopian Investment Holdings.

He rejected the model of shipping African raw materials and jobs abroad. Instead, he said, Dangote aims to bring jobs and value addition to Ethiopia, turn local resources into value-added products for export, and help make the continent self-sufficient.

Dangote also set out the scale of his ambitions beyond Ethiopia. The Lagos refinery is set to expand to 1.4 million barrels a day, and the group plans to invest in 10,000 megawatts of power generation across the continent. He said the group expects $36 billion in revenue by the end of this year and aims to pay off all its debt by this October.

“African enterprises financed by Africans”

Ethiopian officials welcomed the offer as a step toward a more connected African financial system.

Ahmed Shide Speaker of Ethiopian Parliament described the deal as a model of “African enterprises financed by Africans.” He pointed to Dangote’s fertilizer investment in Ethiopia and to the value of interconnected financial markets across the continent, and thanked Dangote for opening the investment to Ethiopian investors.

Dagmawit Shifera said the offer creates a real opportunity for Ethiopia’s qualified investors and advances the interconnection of African capital markets.

On behalf of the exchange, speakers thanked Dangote for choosing the Ethiopian market, calling it a sign of confidence in the country’s capital market and a contribution to a stronger financial sector. They described the ESX as a fair and trusted market where Ethiopian investors can now share in the growth of one of Africa’s largest companies.

Who can invest in Ethiopia?

For the first time, the Ethiopian Capital Market Authority (ECMA) has exempted a foreign company — Dangote Petroleum Refinery — from registration so it can offer shares to investors in Ethiopia. The condition: only qualified investors may buy.

A milestone for a young market

The roadshow is part of a pan-African push by Dangote to build a shareholder base across the continent. The refinery’s IPO, priced at ₦525 per share, seeks to raise about $1.6 billion, with proceeds going toward doubling capacity. The wider offer closes on 27 October, and trading on the Nigerian Exchange is expected to begin in early December.

Under ECMA’s notice issued on 13 October, participation in Ethiopia is capped at 100 qualified investors unless the Authority approves more, and the shares may not be marketed to the general public.

For the ESX, which opened in January 2025 as Ethiopia’s first stock exchange in about half a century, the deal is a landmark: a major African company offering its equity directly to Ethiopian investors. It is also an early test of the interconnected African markets that speakers championed throughout the evening.

art-1792565875312-0mxv3l.title_original: Ethiopia’s Inflation Hits 14.9% in September, Up 1.7 Percentage Points Year on Year
art-1792565875312-0mxv3l.raw_text:
Ethiopia’s annual headline inflation rate eased to 14.9% in September 2026 from 15.1% in August, although it remained above the 13.2% recorded in September last year, according to data released by the Ethiopian Statistical Service (ESS).

The latest figure represents a 1.7 percentage-point increase year on year, indicating that inflationary pressures remain elevated despite a slight month-on-month moderation.

Food and non-alcoholic beverage inflation stood at 14.8% in September, down marginally from 14.9% in August. Sugar, honey and chocolate recorded the highest price increase among food categories, rising 39.8%, compared with 38.3% a month earlier.

Meat prices increased by 22%, while other food products rose by 19.1%. Fruit prices climbed 18.5%, oil and butter rose 18.2%, and milk, dairy products and eggs increased by 17.7%. Vegetable prices went up by 11.4%, while bread and injera, staple foods for Ethiopian households, recorded an 8.6% increase.

Non-food inflation also moderated, falling to 15.1% from 15.4% in August. However, several categories continued to register significant price increases. Alcoholic beverages and tobacco rose by 18.2%, education costs increased by 17.8%, and other goods and services climbed 17.6%. Transport prices rose 16%, while restaurant and hotel costs increased 15.3%.

The September data show mixed movements across non-food categories. Education inflation fell sharply from 25.3% in August to 17.8%, while health inflation declined from 12.8% to 10.9%. Transport inflation edged up from 15.6% to 16%, and alcoholic beverages and tobacco increased from 16% to 18.2%. Communication costs rose from 8% to 9.6%.

Among food items, meat inflation eased from 22.6% in August to 22% in September, while vegetable inflation declined from 12.1% to 11.4%. Bread and injera inflation, however, increased from 8.1% to 8.6%.

Although the decline in the headline rate suggests a modest easing in price pressures, the continued rise in the cost of essential goods and services remains a concern for households. With food inflation at 14.8% and non-food inflation at 15.1%, price increases continue to affect both daily consumption and broader household spending.

The September figures suggest that inflation is cooling slightly compared with the previous month, but the rate remains higher than a year ago, with sharp increases in selected food items continuing to put pressure on the cost of living.

The post Ethiopia’s Inflation Hits 14.9% in September, Up 1.7 Percentage Points Year on Year appeared first on StockMarket.et.

art-1792565875312-zggtcp.title_original: Ethiopia’s Expanded FX Auction Programme Opens Oversubscribed as Demand Returns
art-1792565875312-zggtcp.raw_text:
The National Bank of Ethiopia (NBE) sold USD 140 million to commercial banks on Tuesday at Foreign Exchange Auction No. 30. It was the first sale under the central bank’s enlarged second-quarter programme, and bank demand came in above the amount on offer, after two straight auctions that fell short.

Banks bid a total of USD 152.09 million against the USD 140 million available, so the auction was oversubscribed by about USD 12.09 million, or roughly 8.6%. Twenty-nine banks took part and 26 of them received allocations. The marginal (cut-off) rate was 158.1724 birr per dollar. The weighted average rate of successful bids was 160.1072 birr. Bids ran from a low of 153.0000 to a high of 160.9878 birr per dollar.

A turn from September’s weak demand

The result reverses the pattern of the previous two rounds. At Auction No. 29, the central bank offered USD 125 million and banks bid USD 123.49 million, leaving it undersubscribed by USD 1.51 million. The September 9 auction had also gone unfilled, with $5 million of the $125 million left unsold. That was the first time since the NBE began publishing results that banks did not absorb the full supply. Analysts blamed that shortfall on temporary birr liquidity constraints at banks rather than a structural drop in demand for foreign exchange.

Pricing barely moved. Tuesday’s weighted average of 160.1072 birr was slightly below the 160.2297 recorded at Auction No. 29, which suggests a marginally firmer birr in the official auction. The cut-off rate rose by about 0.10 birr. The auction was also less concentrated than in earlier months. In one round earlier this year, only 9 banks won allocations in a USD 70 million auction, with bids topping out at 158.5 birr per dollar.

A larger quarterly programme

Tuesday’s sale opens a significantly bigger supply calendar. The NBE is allocating $840 million in the second quarter of the 2026/27 fiscal year through six bi-weekly rounds of $140 million each, 12% more per auction than the $125 million offered in Q1. The quarterly total is 68% higher than the regular first-quarter allocation. The remaining auctions are set for October 27, November 10 and 24, and December 8 and 22.

The first quarter included heavy intervention. The NBE held a $500 million special auction on August 20, after banks bid $470.17 million at the August 12 auction, nearly four times the $125 million on offer, pushing the average rate to 161.79 birr per dollar.

Reform backdrop

The auctions are part of reforms that followed the July 2024 move to a market-determined exchange rate. These have included changes to export-proceeds rules, forward FX transactions, and foreign currency retention accounts. An automated interbank FX trading platform also launched at the Ethiopian Securities Exchange in January 2026. The programme is backed by the IMF, whose board approved the fifth review on July 1, 2026, releasing about $464 million and bringing total disbursements to roughly $2.65 billion.

The pressure on demand is large. Ethiopia is projected to import $25.8 billion of goods in 2026/27, with fuel alone accounting for about $6 billion.

The next auction, No. 31, is scheduled for October 27 and will test whether Tuesday’s recovery in demand holds as the larger allocations continue.

The post Ethiopia’s Expanded FX Auction Programme Opens Oversubscribed as Demand Returns appeared first on StockMarket.et.

art-1792565875313-4ft2rx.title_original: Ethiopia opens door to Dangote IPO for qualified investors
art-1792565875313-4ft2rx.raw_text:
The Ethiopian Capital Market Authority (ECMA) said any marketing or sale of Dangote Petroleum Refinery and Petrochemicals shares in Ethiopia must be limited to qualified investors. The ruling keeps Ethiopian retail investors out of what has been billed as Africa’s largest initial public offering.

In a public notice issued on Tuesday, the regulator said it had been approached about a proposed offering in Ethiopia of the Nigerian refiner’s securities as part of its IPO. It said the offer “does not constitute an offer to the general public in Ethiopia.” The shares may not be advertised, marketed, distributed or sold to anyone who does not meet the qualified investor definition under Ethiopian capital market law.

ECMA cited the Capital Market Proclamation No. 1248/2021 and the Public Offer and Trading of Securities Directive No. 1030/2024 as the governing framework.

Conditions for intermediaries

The notice sets out obligations for any capital market service provider, intermediary, representative or agent involved in distributing or placing the securities. They must:

  • direct the offer only to persons who meet the qualified investor requirements
  • cap participation at 100 qualified investors unless the Authority gives prior approval
  • verify and document each investor’s qualified status before that investor participates
  • state clearly in all offering documents and promotional material that the offering is restricted to qualified investors
  • obtain ECMA approval for any solicitation advertisement before it is published, as required by Article 53 of Directive 1030/2024
  • avoid general solicitation, mass marketing or public advertising that could reach non-qualified investors

ECMA also stressed that authorizing a qualified-investor offering is not an endorsement of the securities, the issuer, the IPO or its investment merits. It said investors are responsible for reviewing the offering documents and assessing the risks themselves.

The regulator warned that any offer, solicitation, advertisement or sale of the shares to the general public in Ethiopia without the required registration, approval or exemption may break the law and lead to regulatory action. It advised investors to deal only with persons authorized to carry out capital market activities in Ethiopia.

Africa’s largest IPO

Aliko Dangote formally opened the refinery’s IPO on the Nigerian Exchange (NGX) in Lagos on September 14, 2026. The offer comprises 4.1 billion new ordinary shares priced at N525 each. The sale could raise ₦2.15 trillion, or about $1.6 billion, making it Africa’s largest IPO, and values the refinery at about $47 billion. The offer is open to retail and institutional investors as well as eligible investors across Africa.

The refinery reported $1.82 billion in profit after tax in the first half of 2026 on revenue of more than $13 billion, reversing a $476 million loss in 2025. The IPO follows a $2.5 billion private placement in July that was 3.7 times subscribed. Dangote plans to spend $14.3 billion to double capacity to 1.4 million barrels a day by 2029. The group is also planning a 700,000-barrel-a-day refinery in Kenya and is considering other African listings for the Nigerian refinery after its Lagos debut.

The post Ethiopia opens door to Dangote IPO for qualified investors appeared first on StockMarket.et.

art-1792565875313-2380jg.title_original: KEFI Resumes Development at Ethiopia’s Tulu Kapi Gold Project After Fatal Incident
art-1792565875313-2380jg.raw_text:
KEFI Gold and Copper has resumed development activities at its flagship Tulu Kapi Gold Project in Ethiopia following a temporary suspension triggered by a fatal incident in September 2026.

The company said development was halted after the incident, which it called the “Genji Incident,” began on September 4 and was resolved on September 10 following engagement with local community leaders.

According to KEFI, the incident resulted in the first fatality involving its personnel during the company’s 12 years of involvement in the project.

During the suspension, KEFI’s senior management held consultations with community representatives, federal and Oromia regional government officials, security agencies and other stakeholders. Discussions focused on community welfare, employment, security and workplace safety.

“We are enjoying huge support from all stakeholders and are now restarting development with a phased and measured approach in which we reinforce the emphasis on safety and community benefits,” said Harry Anagnostaras-Adams, KEFI’s executive chairman.

The company said the restart would begin with reconnecting the project site to the regional electricity grid and remobilizing civil engineering teams to construct essential access roads.

Subsequent phases will include resettlement arrangements, including replacement housing and land for communities within the mining licence area, as well as security infrastructure upgrades, major earthworks for the processing plant and permanent staff accommodation.

KEFI expects the project to directly employ approximately 1,000 people from local communities once the mine reaches active production. The company also anticipates opportunities for local businesses and improvements to infrastructure, including roads, electricity connections, schools and healthcare facilities.

International specialists and contractors involved in the project will prioritize local businesses with established operational experience in Oromia, KEFI said.

The resumption follows a mining services agreement signed with BCM Group in June 2026, valued at more than $400 million, to support operations at Tulu Kapi.

KEFI added that international lenders remained committed to the project as discussions continued on revised development timelines and financing arrangements.

The Tulu Kapi project is one of Ethiopia’s major gold development projects, with its progress closely tied to the country’s efforts to expand mining investment and increase the contribution of the mining sector to the economy.

art-1792565875314-h6vci6.title_original: How Two Economists Taught Policymakers to Steer by the Future
art-1792565875314-h6vci6.raw_text:
Robert E. Hall of Stanford University and Michael Woodford of Columbia University have won this year’s Nobel-memorial prize in economics. The Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences honoured them “for microeconomic foundations of macroeconomic stabilisation.”

In plain words: they showed governments and central banks how to calm an economy that is overheating or sliding into recession. Their tools now sit at the heart of the models that policymakers use around the world.

To understand why that matters, you have to go back to a time when those tools seemed broken.

When the old map stopped working

Every economy moves in waves. Good years bring jobs and rising spending. Bad years bring layoffs and closed shops.

For most of the 20th century, policymakers followed a recipe from the economist John Maynard Keynes. In a slump, cut interest rates and let the government spend more than it collects. In a boom, do the opposite and cool things down.

Then came the oil crises of the 1970s, and the recipe failed. The old models promised that a bit more inflation would buy lower unemployment. Instead, Western countries got both at once: prices rose out of control while jobs vanished and growth stalled.

A whole decade went by like this. Many people concluded that trying to steer the economy did more harm than good, and that governments should simply stop trying.

Rebuilding the engine from the inside

Hall and Woodford took a different path. They argued the old models broke because they were built on the wrong thing.

Those models leaned on statistical patterns between big numbers like inflation, output and consumption. When the world changed, the patterns changed too, and the models had nothing deeper to fall back on.

So the laureates started from the bottom: real households and real businesses. How does a family decide how much to spend or save? How does a company decide what price to charge? Add up millions of those choices and you get the whole economy.

Think of it like traffic. You can study rush-hour charts, but they won’t tell you what happens when a new bridge opens. To predict that, you need to understand why each driver picks a route. These are the “microeconomic foundations” in the prize citation.

People look ahead, and that changes everything

The heart of their models is a simple truth: people plan for the future. A family saving for next year, or a firm setting prices for the coming months, acts on what it expects to happen.

That opens a powerful door for policymakers. If a central bank clearly explains what it plans to do with interest rates, people adjust their choices today. Words become a policy tool in their own right.

Picture a captain who announces the course well in advance. The crew starts adjusting before the ship even turns, and the voyage runs smoother. Clear, credible plans can move the economy in the right direction before a single rate is changed.

Two scientists, two pieces of the puzzle

Robert Hall: how households spend. In a famous 1978 paper, Hall showed that if people plan their spending sensibly, future changes in their consumption can’t be predicted from the past. Families already use everything they know; only real surprises shift their plans. This idea changed how economists model households, and Hall went on to study how jobs, wages and unemployment respond to shocks.

Michael Woodford: how prices and central banks interact. Woodford built the full framework for modern monetary policy, laid out in his influential 2003 book Interest and Prices. He showed how firms that set prices with an eye on the future respond to a central bank’s plans. His work explains why clear communication, often called “forward guidance” can be as important as the interest rate itself.

Together, their work gave the so-called New Keynesian models a solid footing. Keynes’s goal of smoothing booms and busts survived, but now it rested on how real people actually behave.

Today, central banks and finance ministries around the world use models built on these ideas. When an energy crisis hits, or households suddenly cut back on spending, these models help decide how hard and how fast to respond.

“The laureates’ work has provided us with a stable theoretical foundation for the models that are now used by central banks and governments around the world,” said John Hassler, Chair of the Committee for the Prize in Economic Sciences.

The result is an economy with gentler peaks and shallower troughs. For ordinary people, that can mean fewer lost jobs in hard times and steadier prices in good ones. Half a century after stabilisation policy nearly died, Hall and Woodford helped bring it back to life.

art-1792565875315-hz9dxe.title_original: Dagmawit Shiferaw Takes the Helm at ECMA as Hana Tehelku Moves to Investment Commission
art-1792565875315-hz9dxe.raw_text:
Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed has appointed Dagmawit Shiferaw as Director General of the Ethiopian Capital Market Authority, replacing Hana Tehelku, who moves to lead the Ethiopian Investment Commission as part of a wider reshuffle of senior economic posts. Yirgalem Assefa (PhD) has been named Deputy Director General of ECMA.

The appointments place new leadership at both the capital market regulator and the country’s principal investment promotion agency at the same moment, and the timing is deliberate. ECMA and the EIC are the two institutions most directly responsible for translating Ethiopia’s economic liberalisation agenda into real capital flows, and the government is rotating experienced people through both.

Dagmawit brings more than 15 years of experience spanning investment management, innovative finance, telecommunications, consulting, and public sector leadership. Her career includes roles at UNDP, Renew Capital, STGT Trading, Candor Consultancy, and Ethio Telecom. Since 2023 she has served as Director of the Innovative Finance Lab at UNDP Ethiopia, where she led technical strategy, stakeholder coordination, resource mobilisation, and knowledge management. Her background in innovative finance is a reasonable fit for a regulator that is still building the market infrastructure for instruments such as green bonds, gender bonds, and eventually ETFs and REITs, whose enabling directive took effect last month.

Hana Tehelku leaves ECMA after leading it since August 2024, following the tenure of Brook Taye, the authority’s founding Director General. Under her watch the Ethiopian Securities Exchange launched in January 2025, the first foreign investment bank received its license by mid-2026, and the registration pipeline expanded to cover banks, insurance companies, and cooperative financial institutions across the country. ECMA now oversees 26 registered companies, seven of them active in the securities market.

At the EIC, Hana takes over from Zeleke Temesgen, who moves to Ethiopian Investment Holdings as Deputy CEO. Melekit Sahlu and Baysa Bedada (PhD) have been appointed Deputy Commissioners at the EIC. Jafar Bedru joins Zeleke as a second Deputy CEO at EIH, giving the state holding company two new senior executives as part of the same reshuffle.

The leadership change at ECMA comes at a moment of real momentum. The ESX mainboard currently lists five equities, the eurobond restructuring reached a preliminary agreement in July, and the IMF’s fifth ECF review confirmed continued progress on macroeconomic stabilisation. The regulatory calendar ahead includes deepening OTC market participation, expanding the investment bank roster, and building the supervisory framework for the collective investment scheme instruments that are now legally permitted.

Dagmawit inherits an authority that has done the harder early work of building from nothing. The next phase is consolidation, credibility, and depth.

Source: Prime Minister’s Office

art-1792565875315-tfvpto.title_original: Oromia Bank Launches Three Tiers of International Visa Payment Cards
art-1792565875315-tfvpto.raw_text:
Oromia Bank has officially launched three tiers of international Visa payment cards, expanding its services to customers seeking to make payments abroad and conduct international online transactions.

The cards, unveiled at Skylight Hotel, include the Oro Visa Classic, Oro Visa Gold, and Oro Visa Platinum. The bank introduced the services in partnership with Visa, a global digital payments company, and Premier Switch Solutions (PSS), Ethiopia’s first Visa-certified third-party payment processor.

Speaking at the launch ceremony, Oromia Bank CEO Teferi Mekonnen said the new cards would expand customers’ international payment options alongside the bank’s existing card services. He added that the products were designed to address customer needs and could be used at payment locations accepting the Visa network.

Oromia Bank Board Chairperson Assefa Seme said that providing modern digital financial services had become an obligation as the world increasingly shifts toward digitalization.

Visa East Africa Cluster Head and Ethiopia Country Manager Yared Endale and PSS Group CEO Ameha Tadesse also reaffirmed their commitment to strengthening their partnership with Oromia Bank.

The three card tiers target customers who need to make international payments for travel, education, business, online shopping, and other e-commerce transactions.
